opus-5.5.text:
I think coverage matters more than whether the data is real or virtual. People spend a lot of energy debating sim versus real, but the more fundamental question is whether your training data covers the situations the robot will actually face when deployed.

If you think of it as a distribution problem, a learned policy is good at interpolating within what it has seen and quite poor at extrapolating outside it. So if your data covers the relevant states, objects, lighting conditions, contact dynamics and failure cases, the policy tends to work. If it doesn't, the policy fails, and it fails whether the missing data would have come from simulation or from the real world. The source is secondary. The coverage is primary.

Real data and simulated data each have strengths and weaknesses along that axis. Real-world data has no reality gap. The physics, the sensor noise and the visual appearance are exactly what the robot will see. But it's expensive and slow to collect, and it's very hard to get coverage of rare or dangerous situations. You don't want a robot falling down a thousand times to learn recovery, and you can't easily stage every corner case in a lab. So real data tends to be high fidelity but narrow.

Simulation is the opposite. It's cheap, parallelizable and safe, and you can deliberately push into the long tail: randomize friction, masses, textures, camera positions, terrain. That's why domain randomization worked so well for locomotion. We weren't making the simulator perfectly accurate. We were making the training distribution broad enough that the real world became just one more sample inside it. The downside is that simulation has systematic gaps, especially in contact-rich manipulation, deformable objects, and visual realism. If the simulator never produces a certain phenomenon, no amount of randomization will cover it.

So in practice I see them as complementary tools for the same goal, which is maximizing useful coverage. For locomotion, simulation alone already gives good enough coverage, and sim-to-real works remarkably well. For manipulation and more open-ended tasks, we rely much more on real-world data, including large-scale teleoperation, and increasingly on data that isn't robot data at all, like internet video and language. Those bring in semantic and world knowledge that neither a simulator nor a lab collection effort can easily provide.

Looking forward, the line between real and virtual is getting blurrier. Generative models and learned world models can produce synthetic experience that's grounded in real data, and real data can be augmented in simulation. So I'd encourage people to stop asking "is this real or fake?" and instead ask "where are the holes in my data distribution, and what's the cheapest way to fill them?" Sometimes the answer is a simulator, sometimes it's a teleoperator, and sometimes it's a video model. Coverage is what ultimately determines generalization.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says coverage matters more than whether training data is real or virtual, and calls the data source secondary to coverage.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer directly as the guest, no tools needed.

Jie Tan: I think coverage matters more than whether the data is real or simulated, and that's actually a somewhat contrarian view in the field. People often assume real data is inherently better because it has no sim-to-real gap. But what a robot policy actually needs is to have seen the situations it will encounter at deployment. If your real dataset only covers a few kitchens, a few lighting conditions, a few object poses, then it doesn't matter how "real" it is. The robot will fail the moment it walks into a room it hasn't seen.

Simulation gives you something real data can't easily give you, which is the ability to sweep the space. You can randomize friction, mass, lighting, textures, object geometry, and you can generate millions of episodes overnight. That's where domain randomization came from in our locomotion work. We weren't trying to make simulation perfectly match reality. We were trying to make the distribution wide enough that reality fell somewhere inside it. And the legged robots that learned this way transferred remarkably well, even to terrains we never explicitly modeled.

That said, I don't think it's either-or. There are parts of the physics, like contact dynamics and deformable objects, where our simulators are still quite rough. Real data anchors you to those details. So the way I think about it is: real data tells you where the distribution is, and simulation lets you cover it. A small amount of real data to calibrate, and a large amount of simulated data to fill in the long tail. The teams that get the balance right are the ones whose robots generalize.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says coverage matters more than whether training data is real or simulated, and explains that deployment situations must be represented in the data.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether the training data covers the situations the robot will encounter. Whether that data comes from the real world or from simulation is important, but it’s not the whole story. Real-world data can still be very narrow. If you collect everything in one environment under similar conditions, the robot may struggle when those conditions change.

Simulation gives us a way to broaden that coverage. We can vary the environment, physical parameters, and disturbances, and expose the robot to situations that would be difficult or expensive to collect in reality. But diversity alone isn’t enough—the variation has to be relevant to deployment. If the simulator misses an important aspect of the real world, generating more data won’t necessarily solve that problem.

So I would focus on coverage first, while checking that what the robot learns transfers to reality. Real-world testing can reveal the gaps, and then we can use both simulation and real data to fill them. They’re complementary tools for building a robot that works beyond its training conditions.

r001.rationale: The response says the key question is whether data covers situations the robot will encounter and that coverage should come first; it treats real versus simulated data as important but secondary.

sol-6.1.text:
I think coverage is often more important than whether the data comes from the real world or simulation. What matters is whether the robot encounters enough variation during training to handle the situations it will face when deployed.

Real-world data is valuable, but it can still be narrow. If you collect everything with one robot in one environment, the policy may work very well there and fail when conditions change. Simulation lets you vary things like friction, payload, sensor noise, and disturbances much more broadly, including situations that would be expensive or risky to collect on a real robot.

Of course, coverage alone is not enough if the simulator misses something essential about the real world. So I see these as complementary: use simulation to get broad coverage, and use real-world experiments to identify the gaps and improve the training distribution. The goal is data that prepares the robot for deployment.

r001.rationale: It explicitly says coverage is often more important than whether training data comes from the real world or simulation.
